The Drews here live separately but not isolated preserving their language beliefs and ancient [music] rituals. Its almost perfect circular shape offers a supernatural feeling like a mirror reflecting both fire and ice. In winter, the lake freezes, transforming the landscape into a scene of glass and stillness. In summer, it becomes a refuge for herds of livestock. Locals whisper that the lake has no end. That beneath its placid surface lies a secret passage leading into the heart of the mountain. Bring water from hills tens of kilometers away using only stone and gravity. The limestone arches still stand stretching along the coast where waves break against their bases as if reminding us of the water that once flowed through them. In the evening light, the salt encrusted ruins glow with an ancient bronze hue. The only metal that time cannot corrode. These Roman aqueducts stand firm to this day, over 2,000 years later. A testament to the engineering genius of ancient Romans. Cesaria's Roman theater faces the sea a luxury and also a metaphor for impermanence. An open air amphitheater built in the 1st century BCE. Its stone seating curves like a sea shell and its open arch captures winds from the ocean. This semi-ircular structure with a capacity for 4,000 people is still preserved and hosts performances offering superb acoustics and a glimpse into Roman entertainment often enlivened by modern concerts or plays. It was once believed that King Solomon mined copper here and that at the foot of these pillars, Egyptian metallurgists lit fires to worship the goddess Hathor, the goddess of copper and the desert. The remnants of smelters and copper fragments make this place both a mining site and a petrified temple. Rock formations shaped like mushrooms arches or naturally carved cliffs. In [music] the distance, a hidden body of water, the artificial Timna Lake, its emerald green hue, stands out against the Rocky Mountains, making the beauty of this place even more mysterious. The sky suddenly feels lower as if pulled down by the weight of stone and silence. Here, the heat doesn't just burn the skin. It forges human faith into an unyielding metal. The path leading up to the fortress is winding and endless with sand and stone. At the end of the path, a towering mountain emerges. Without prior introduction, few could imagine a unique fortress [music] spanning thousands of meters a top that 400 m high peak. Msada is a profound symbol of humanity's continuous struggle between oppression and freedom. Heading east, the road winds through rock and dust to Marsaba Monastery, a stone mirage clinging to the cliff face. [music] Teared stone walls cling [music] tightly to the sheer rock face, making the entire structure appear to grow out of the very hillside. The pale yellow desert stone [music] blends with dark copper domes, creating a spectacle that is both majestic and surreal. [music] The tradition here still maintains the rule. Women are not allowed into the monastery, only able to view it from the opposite side of the canyon. Yet every breath echoes like a dialogue with God. Looking into the distance, Wadi Kelt Canyon opens like a green crack in the fiery rock. From deep within the earth, tiny springs trickle [music] into streams flowing around St. George's Monastery, where the sound of bells rings down the valley, blending with the sound of water, a rare symphony amidst drought and life. Bedawin riders slowly move along ancient trails. Their small figures against the giant cliffs evoke a sense that time has never passed. Finally, Kumran, where silent stones once held prophecies. The caves, where the Dead Sea Scrolls were hidden, where the Essenes lived in solitude, awaiting the apocalypse with quiet faith. And sometimes when the Judeian wind blows through, one can still hear a soft rustling like paper, as if undiscovered scrolls are still stirring in the sand. Following the Mediterranean coast opens up another world, Hifer, a city of light and [music] green. On the slopes of Mount Carmel, overlooking the Mediterranean, the Bahay Gardens emerge like a symphony of order and tranquility. 19 perfectly manicured terraces stretch from the base to the summit. Each level like a note in the harmonious song [music] between humanity and nature. At its heart, the shrine of the Babu with its glittering golden dome, the resting place of the Bab. The prophet who pioneered the Bahasu faith shines like a small sun amidst a sea of trees and white [music] stone. viewed from above, the garden is arranged with almost mathematical precision. Impeccably trimmed green hedges, gurgling fountains, seasonal flowers, concentric circles, and paved paths guiding the gaze directly towards the sea. This is considered a symbol of belief in harmony between humanity, nature, and God. A place where every step feels like crossing the boundary between the material and the spiritual. Here every hill, every stone is an unclosed chapter of human history. And though religion, culture or borders may divide people, nature silently connects all with wind, with sand, with memory. Israel is not just a place to see, but to listen, where the past still breathes [music] and every step touches something sacred that has never been lost.
